metadata.persona: Shubham Bagwe (script written with Claude, synthetic voice)
metadata.bookend_exempt_reason: Course pitch, not a channel explainer. The assignment says to narrate as myself and not use the instructor's name, persona or credit line, so there is no Liam greeting, no hesitant-writer/terms cards, no Your Turn composer (a pitch has no viewer exercise), and no verdict card; B15 states exists vs will-exist instead. The outro is kept, as my own drawn beat.

beats.narration_text: I'm Shubham Baag-way, and this is my final project pitch, written with Claude and spoken by a synthetic voice. Marino Desk Assistant will answer front-desk questions at Northeastern's Marino Recreation Center, like fees, hours and guest rules, from the public recreation website, and quote the page it used.

beats.narration_text: When it's done, it will be a public GitHub repository: a Python and FastAPI backend, a Next.js chat window, Claude writing the answers, and an evaluation report. A first version already exists, and its sixty tests passed today.

beats.narration_text: Here's the problem. A member at the desk asks what an alumni membership costs. The answer is on the website, inside a page of about eight hundred words of fee tables, while the member waits.

beats.narration_text: I looked at what we use now. The site's own search returns pages, not answers. A search for guest pass today returned five pages, with the home page first. Manual lookup means scrolling until you find the line.

beats.narration_text: Mine will save the desk assistant that scroll. It will give one answer, quote the exact line, and link to it, which the site search doesn't do. And when the website doesn't say, it will answer: I don't know.

beats.narration_text: My target role is new-grad full-stack engineer, so my reader is a hiring manager or an engineer. In sixty seconds, they'll see the evaluation table in the read-me, run one command, ask a fee question, and watch it refuse an off-topic one.

beats.assignment_question: Q4 what it proves: grounding + contract
beats.narration_text: What will it prove? Source grounding: it already retrieves five passages and reranks them to three. Next, a prompt contract: Claude must return the answer, the quoted line, the link and the date, and a quote that isn't in the page fails.

beats.narration_text: And evaluation: fifty real desk questions with my own answer keys, scored three ways. Did it cite the right page? Was the answer right? Did it refuse when it should? Every miss goes in the report.

beats.narration_text: A reviewer could fairly conclude that I can specify, ground and evaluate an AI app, and measure where it's wrong. Not that it's always accurate, and not that Marino uses it officially.

beats.narration_text: What's in: the public recreation pages, with fees, hours and policies. Deliberately out: internal staff documents. They aren't public, so the finished repo never indexes them. It also won't check live court availability.

beats.narration_text: What could sink it? Prices that depend on the date. Today, the alumni page lists five yearly prices for the same membership, from four hundred eighty dollars in September down to one hundred twenty in June. A model that doesn't know today's date can quote the wrong one, confidently.

beats.narration_text: So the contract will pass in today's date and require the quoted row, the evaluation will include date questions, and every answer will show its crawl date. The limit I can't fix: it's only as current as the last crawl.

beats.narration_text: Why this project? I work the Marino front desk, and these are the questions I get. It's a mix. Backend and cloud I already have: I wrote the EventFlow Engine myself, a Node pipeline on Google Cloud. The Marino repo's current code was mostly AI-generated under my direction, so it isn't my proof. New to me: answer keys, measuring a model's misses, and prompt contracts.
